newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia seeks compromise -- at home and abroad.
newsitem.headline: Russia seeks compromise -- at home and abroad.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, whose job looks secure despite Boris Yeltsin's looming government reshuffle, flies to Washington on Saturday to prepare the president's Helsinki summit with Bill Clinton.

The Kremlin said on Friday, more than a week after Yeltsin ordered sweeping government changes to tackle a deepening social crisis, that details of the reshuffle would finally be announced before Yeltsin heads for Finland on Wednesday.

Primakov will be seeking to lay the ground for a deal with the U.S. president that could lead to a compromise on NATO's expansion plans. Yeltsin said on Friday the March 19-20 summit would be his toughest ever but that compromise was possible.

There may also be compromise -- this time between Russia's reformers and Yeltsin's more conservative allies -- when the president unveils his new government team after meeting Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday or Tuesday.
The foreign ministry has said Primakov has proposals to make in the row with NATO over its plans to offer membership to Moscow's former communist allies in eastern and central Europe.
Primakov, who meets Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Saturday, Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday and Clinton on Monday, also expects serious discussion on arms control.

Helsinki will be a chance for Yeltsin, 66, to show he has recovered after eight months of heart trouble and pneumonia. He even got the chance to turn the tables and send get well wishes to Clinton, who had an operation on his injured knee on Friday.
The Kremlin leader says he is determined to take Russia's international and domestic problems in hand.

But the time taken to form the new government since he handed a leading role a week ago to his liberal chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais has fuelled speculation that cutting out dead wood and creating a streamlined pro-reform team is proving hard.

Indications from Yeltsin that the upper ranks of the cabinet may be fuller than expected was also seen by some analysts as a sign he may be slow to alienate faithful supporters for the sake of the new approach Chubais is believed to be seeking.
Yeltsin said on Friday there would, in addition to Chubais as sole first deputy premier, be seven deputy premiers. There are three first deputies and nine deputies in the present team.

Chernomyrdin was ordered by Yeltsin to get rid of much of the government he formed only in August. Kremlin sources say Chubais, who is hated by the communists for privatising Russian industry, wants a free hand to push through more market reforms.
But there are more conservative voices around Yeltsin, too, notably among Russia's big industrialists who see Chernomyrdin, a former gas industry chief, as a guarantor of their interests.
Chubais, 41, is said to want to reduce the influence of ministries whose close relationships with the industries they regulate is a hangover from the days of Soviet central planning.
Yeltsin has shown time and again his propensity to play his various groups of supporters off against each other, so the eventual cabinet line-up may well represent a balance of forces.
Despite the time taken to announce the new government, there is an urgency in the situation. A week after returning from Helsinki, Yeltsin will face a nationwide strike on March 27.

Former Kremlin security chief General Alexander Lebed warned on Friday that discontent over unpaid wages and pensions could boil over into Albanian-style anarchy. Lebed is demanding new elections, which opinion polls suggest he could well win.
Fortunately for Yeltsin, however, his recovery makes an early vote less likely, although the communists too renewed demands on Friday for him to step down on health grounds.

A poll by the VTsIOM research institute showed that eight months into his second term, 20 percent of Russians approved of Yeltsin's record and 79 percent disapproved. Ominously, Chubais was even more unpopular, with an 85-percent disapproval rating.
